summary.text: Manorialism was the method of land ownership in parts of Europe, notably France and later England, during the Middle Ages.
A lord and his dependents lived in a manor house or castle and ran a rural estate, while labourers or serfs worked the surrounding land to support themselves and the lord.
It was part of the feudal system, and it was slowly replaced by a money-based market economy and new forms of agrarian contract.

items.prompt: In the early Middle Ages a farm worker hands part of his harvest to the lord. Centuries later, his descendant pays the lord in coins instead. What lies behind the change?

options.label: Growing commercial activity
Lords no longer needed food once they left their manors
Farm work was no longer needed on the estate
Churches took over all grain collection from lords

items.explain: Labourers first paid with labour time or produce, and later paid in cash as commercial activity increased.

items.prompt: A historian looks for the ancestor of the medieval manor system. Where do its antecedents lead?

options.label: The longhouses of Viking settlers
The city-states of ancient Greece
The rural economy of the later Roman Empire
The courts of early Islamic caliphs

items.explain: Manorialism originated in the Roman villa system, and its antecedents can be traced to the rural economy of the later Roman Empire.

items.prompt: Late Roman officials froze society in place: sons followed their fathers' trades, and cultivators could not leave the land they were attached to. Where was this heading for the workers of the land?

options.label: They were on their way to owning land outright
They were on their way to serving as paid soldiers
They were on their way to running market towns
They were on their way to becoming serfs

items.explain: Because cultivators were tied to the land, the workers of the land were on their way to becoming serfs.

items.prompt: Serfs are gone from an estate, yet the lord still runs it with freehold labourers. What does this show about the manor system?

options.label: It had already vanished with the serfs
It could carry on after serfdom ended
It had turned into a military order
It could only work on royal land

items.explain: Manorialism outlasted serfdom in the sense that it continued with freehold labourers.

items.prompt: Which sight in the countryside was the most vivid feature of manorialism, and faded away along with it?

options.label: The open field system, with strips of land worked individually
Stone aqueducts carrying water to each village
Walled monasteries standing beside every estate
Rows of watchtowers along every border

items.explain: Manorialism faded slowly alongside its most vivid feature in the landscape, the open field system, where strips of land were individually worked.

items.prompt: An abbey holds a seigneurie, and a bailiff handles much of its business. What does this show about who could be a lord and how a lord's power worked?

options.label: Only individual nobles could be lords, and always ruled in person
Only the king could be a lord, and bailiffs held no power
A lord could be an institution, and power ran through intermediaries
Lords were chosen by villagers, who then picked a bailiff

items.explain: A lord could be an individual or an ecclesiastical institution such as an abbey, and the lord's power was exercised through intermediaries, most importantly the bailiff.

paragraphs.heading: The manor and its people
paragraphs.text: Manorialism, also called seigneurialism or the manor system, was a way of holding land, known as tenure, in parts of medieval Europe, especially France and later England. At its centre stood a large manor house or castle, sometimes fortified, where the lord and his dependants lived and ran a country estate. Around it, labourers or serfs worked the land to feed themselves and the lord. They paid their dues at first in work time or in produce, and later in cash as trade grew. Manorialism was one part of the wider feudal system.

paragraphs.heading: Roman roots
paragraphs.text: The system grew out of the villa estates of the late Roman Empire. There, labour was the key input of production, and governments tried to steady the economy by freezing society in place: sons had to take up their fathers' trades, and coloni, the people who farmed the land, could not leave the land they were tied to. Former slaves and former free farmers merged into one dependent class, so that a person could be called both slave and colonus. Laws of Constantine I around 325 hardened the half-free status of the coloni and limited their right to go to court.

paragraphs.heading: After Rome
paragraphs.text: As Germanic kingdoms took over from Roman authority in the west during the fifth century, Germanic landlords often simply stepped into the place of Roman ones, with little change underneath. In old Roman settlements, the villa system of late antiquity passed into the medieval world. Then in the eighth century, when normal Mediterranean trade was disrupted, the countryside was pushed hard toward feeding itself.

paragraphs.heading: Lords and their courts
paragraphs.text: A manor, or seigneurie, was a local unit of land and justice under a lord (in French, seigneur), who usually held it in return for promises to a higher lord. The lord held a manorial court that followed public law and local custom. Lords were not always laymen: bishops and abbots held lands with similar duties, and an abbey, a cathedral chapter or a military order could be a lord too. The lord's power was carried out through agents, the most important being the bailiff.

paragraphs.heading: A new kind of grant
paragraphs.text: Before manors, land was held in one of two ways: most often allodially, in full outright ownership, or as precaria or benefices, held only on conditions, which is where the English word 'precarious' comes from. The Carolingian kings added a third form, the aprisio, which tied manorialism to feudalism. It first appeared in Septimania in southern France, when Charlemagne had to settle Visigothic refugees who had fled with his army after his failed Zaragoza expedition of 778. He gave them uncultivated 'desert' land belonging to the royal fisc, under his direct control.

paragraphs.heading: Village and manor house
paragraphs.text: A standard plan of a medieval manor shows the strips of separately worked land in the open field system. Sometimes the manor house stood a little apart from the village; just as often the village grew up around its once-walled forecourt, as can still be seen at Petworth House. In the 18th century, as people cared more about privacy, manor houses were often set farther from villages. At Harlaxton Manor in Lincolnshire in the 1830s, the old house at the village edge was abandoned for a new one alone in its park, with the village out of sight.

paragraphs.heading: A slow fade
paragraphs.text: Manorialism faded slowly and piece by piece, giving way to a money-based market economy and new kinds of farming contract, and its open fields went with it. It outlived serfdom, carrying on with freehold labourers. Andrew Jones argues it outlasted feudalism too, since a manor could support a warrior just as well as a capitalist landlord. France's last feudal dues were abolished in the French Revolution, and in parts of eastern Germany the Junkers' Rittergut manors lasted until World War II.
